Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the current imaging shows a partial response with disappearance of three lesions and size reduction of the remaining disease, but the precise anatomical distribution of the residual liver metastases, the estimated future liver remnant (FLR) volume, and relationship to major vascular and biliary structures are not provided. These pieces of information are decisive for determining whether a curative hepatectomy can be performed now or after preparatory measures (e.g., portal vein embolization, staged resection).

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic therapy (FOLFOXIRI or switch to a regimen incorporating targeted agents based on molecular profile) for additional cycles to maximize tumor shrinkage and assess biochemical response (CEA trend).  
- Obtain high‑resolution, contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary phase and volumetric analysis to define residual lesion locations, sizes, and calculate FLR.  
- If lesions are confined to one lobe or can be cleared with a limited resection leaving an adequate FLR (>30 % in normal liver, >40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury suspected), plan for upfront curative hepatectomy after confirming resectability.  
- If lesions are bilobar or FLR is insufficient, consider conversion strategies:  
   • Portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy of the future remnant.  
   • Two‑stage hepatectomy: resect lesions in the future remnant first, allow hypertrophy, then clear remaining disease.  
- Parallel management of the rectal primary: restaging with pelvic MRI; if the primary remains resectable and asymptomatic, schedule low anterior resection after systemic therapy, or deliver neoadjuvant chemoradiation if indicated by T/N stage.  
- Re‑evaluate CEA and imaging after each treatment interval; proceed to surgery once complete (R0) resection of all hepatic disease is deemed feasible and the patient’s performance status and liver function are acceptable.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6‑12 months of systemic therapy, adjusted according to pathological response and molecular markers.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact number, size, and segmental location of residual liver lesions after chemotherapy.  
- Relationship of lesions to major hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
- Volumetric assessment of future liver remnant and baseline liver function (ICG clearance, bilirubin, AST/ALT, platelet count).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status) to guide targeted/immune therapy.  
- Current status of the rectal primary (clinical T/N stage, symptomatology, prior local therapy).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and baseline cardiopulmonary reserve.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After FOLFOXIRI, three lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions show ~40% reduction, with several becoming hypo-intense on MRI. Despite this favorable response, the initial tumor burden and presumed bilobar distribution make immediate R0 resection uncertain without precise segmental mapping and volumetric assessment. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed re-evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging before any decision
• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging and a chest CT scan.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Assessment of true segmental resectability
• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.
• Intra-operative ultrasound will be essential to localize occult residual disease.

C. Surgical strategy if complete clearance is feasible
• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI.
B. Precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
E. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor.
F. a chest CT scan
G. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation
I. Evolution of CEA after first-line chemotherapy.
J. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
Both recommendations are aligned in terms of completeness as they cover major clinical domains like resectability assessment, imaging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative therapy. They both acknowledge the potentially resectable status and emphasize the need for detailed imaging and FLR calculation.

In terms of step-by-step concordance, both recommendations agree on two main steps: assessing resectability post-conversion therapy and proceeding with surgery if feasible. They suggest similar surgical strategies and systemic therapy continuation if resection isn’t immediately possible.

Case-tailoring is not fully aligned. Recommendation 2 emphasizes surgical techniques (e.g., parenchymal-sparing, intra-operative ultrasound) and minimally invasive approaches more than Recommendation 1. Recommendation 1 provides a more detailed oncological strategy and postoperative plan, while Recommendation 2 focuses more on specific surgical planning and ablation strategies.

Both recommendations are concordant regarding missing data, emphasizing the importance of detailed anatomical and molecular data, FLR, and rectal primary status. Recommendation 2 adds details on differentiation grade and liquid biopsies, but these do not substantially alter the essential missing information identified in Recommendation 1.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The current imaging shows three residual hepatic lesions <2 cm after systemic therapy, but critical information required to confirm technical resectability is missing. Specifically, volumetric assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) and precise anatomic relationship of the lesions to major vascular and biliary structures are needed before a definitive surgical plan can be made.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic therapy to deepen response and allow maximal tumor shrinkage. Preferred regimen: oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX or CAPOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type status; consider adding bevacizumab if anti‑EGFR not feasible.  
- After 2–3 additional cycles (total 6–7 cycles), repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted sequences and obtain a contrast‑enhanced CT of the chest/abdomen for comprehensive restaging.  
- Perform quantitative liver volumetry (CT or MRI) to calculate FLR; if FLR <30 % of total liver volume (or <40 % in steatotic liver), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  
- Re‑evaluate the rectal primary: if the primary is clinically stable (no obstructive symptoms, no perforation) and responsive, consider a staged approach—first hepatic resection, then definitive rectal surgery (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection) after recovery. If the primary remains symptomatic or threatens local control, a simultaneous colorectal‑hepatic operation can be contemplated, provided operative risk is acceptable.  
- Surgical plan for the liver: aim for an R0 resection of all three lesions, using parenchymal‑sparing techniques (segmentectomy or wedge resection) whenever possible to preserve liver parenchyma. Intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to confirm lesion margins and detect any occult disease.  
- Post‑operative management: resume adjuvant systemic therapy (total of 12 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy) and consider maintenance anti‑EGFR therapy if disease‑free. Enroll patient in surveillance protocol with serial CEA, imaging at 3‑month intervals for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Exact segmental location of each hepatic lesion and proximity to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
- Quantitative liver function assessment (e.g., ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin, platelet count) and calculated future liver remnant volume.  
- Status of the rectal primary (size, T stage, involvement of mesorectal fascia, response to chemotherapy, presence of symptoms).  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities influencing surgical risk.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease beyond the liver (e.g., lung nodules, peritoneal implants).  
- Details of the chemotherapy regimen already administered (agents, dose intensity, toxicity profile).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI and precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
D. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Status and treatment plan of the rectal primary tumor : Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
G. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
Completeness: Both recommendations address the major clinical domains and management components, including resectability assessment, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative care. They both emphasize the need for further imaging and FLR calculation, and they both propose a systemic therapy strategy before surgical intervention.

Step Concordance: Both recommendations agree on the potential resectability of the liver lesions, pending further detailed assessment. They propose a similar management sequence: continuation of systemic therapy, restaging, and then surgical intervention with options for parenchymal-sparing techniques and consideration of FLR. They also integrate the management of the rectal primary tumor into the overall treatment plan.

Case Tailoring: Recommendation 1 tailors the approach by considering specific chemotherapy regimens (e.g., anti-EGFR agents due to RAS wild-type status) and surgical techniques specific to the patient's liver condition (e.g., FLR assessment and potential PVE/ALPPS). Recommendation 2, while also discussing specific techniques like minimally invasive surgery and prehabilitation, does not overlap entirely with the same case-specific details, such as molecular profiling implications (e.g., RAS status) or specific chemotherapy considerations related to the patient's molecular profile.

Missing Data Concordance: Both recommendations identify critical missing data points, but Recommendation 2 includes additional details regarding molecular profiling (MSS/MSI), liquid biopsies, and rectal tumor specifics, which are not discussed in Recommendation 1. This discrepancy suggests a lack of concordance in recognizing all essential missing data.

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The patient has residual hepatic disease (7 lesions) after systemic therapy, including one lesion that is progressing (5 cm in segment VII).  
- The progressing lesion requires additional local control (e.g., ablative therapy or further chemotherapy) before a definitive liver resection can be contemplated.  
- Definitive assessment of resectability also depends on the anatomic distribution of the remaining lesions, the anticipated future liver remnant, and overall liver function, which are not provided. Therefore surgery cannot be performed upfront, but the disease may become resectable after the prerequisite local treatment and further evaluation.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) to maintain disease control and attempt further downsizing of the progressing segment VII lesion.  
- Apply a locoregional modality to the progressing lesion: percutaneous radiofrequency/ microwave ablation, irreversible electroporation, or stereotactic body radiotherapy, aiming for complete necrosis.  
- Re‑image (contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI) 4–6 weeks after local treatment to assess response of all hepatic lesions and to obtain volumetric data for future liver remnant (FLR).  
- If the FLR is ≥30 % (≥40 % in steatotic or chemotherapy‑injured liver) and all lesions are either resectable or amenable to intra‑operative ablation, plan a parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy:  
   • Use intra‑operative ultrasound to map lesions.  
   • Perform segmental or subsegmental resections of the stable lesions, preserving maximal parenchyma.  
   • Combine with intra‑operative ablation for lesions that are deep or adjacent to major vessels.  
- If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy before definitive resection.  
- Address the primary left‑sided colon tumor: if symptomatic or obstructive, perform colectomy before or after liver surgery; otherwise, schedule a curative colectomy after hepatic clearance.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen) for at least 3 months, tailored to tolerance and pathological response.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Exact location (segmental distribution) and size of each of the six stable hepatic lesions.  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ICG clearance) and presence of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury.  
- Calculated future liver remnant volume after planned resections.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Current status of the primary colon tumor (resected, symptomatic, residual disease).  
- Performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities that may affect surgical risk.  
- Details of the chemotherapy regimen, duration, and toxicity profile.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial, residual, and disappeared lesions and detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment VII lesion.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
E. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Patient’s performance status for potential combined surgical/ablative strategy.
G. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning: The two recommendations cover similar major clinical domains such as the assessment of resectability, systemic therapy, local control, and postoperative considerations, demonstrating completeness in their scope. However, they diverge significantly in the assessment of resectability, with Recommendation 1 considering the disease potentially resectable after local treatment and further evaluation, whereas Recommendation 2 deems the situation as currently unresectable due to the heterogeneous response and suggests selective local strategies only if systemic control is regained. This divergence in the assessment of resectability leads to differences in the proposed management plans, resulting in a lack of step concordance. Case-specific details differ between the recommendations, such as the emphasis on molecular profiling in Recommendation 2, which is absent in Recommendation 1, and the difference in focus on specific surgical techniques. Regarding missing data, both recommendations identify critical information but differ in emphasis and detail, such as the inclusion of molecular profiling and liquid biopsies in Recommendation 2, absent in Recommendation 1, leading to a lack of concordance in missing data identification.

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The current imaging shows a radiologic complete response after FOLFOXIRI, but definitive surgical planning requires (a) high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast (or PET‑CT) to exclude occult residual disease and to precisely map the original bilobar lesion sites, and (b) assessment of hepatic functional reserve (future liver remnant, bilirubin, ICG clearance) and the status of the primary rectal tumor. Until these decisive pieces of information are obtained, a definitive “Resectable upfront” classification cannot be made.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Obtain a liver‑specific MRI (gadoxetate‑enhanced) and a whole‑body PET‑CT to confirm complete metabolic and anatomic response and to delineate the original locations of the metastases.  
- Perform a thorough hepatic functional assessment (CT volumetry for future liver remnant, serum bilirubin, albumin, ICG‑R15) and review the primary rectal tumor (MRI pelvis, endoscopic findings, neoadjuvant radiotherapy status).  
- If imaging confirms no residual disease and liver function is adequate:  
   • Plan a curative‑intent liver surgery targeting the original metastatic sites (anatomic segmental or non‑anatomic resections) to obtain pathological clearance, preferably using intra‑operative ultrasound to guide resection.  
   • Coordinate with colorectal surgery for simultaneous or staged resection of the rectal primary, depending on its response and need for sphincter‑preserving technique.  
   • Consider peri‑operative antibiotics and thromboprophylaxis per standard protocols.  
- If MRI/PET reveals residual disease:  
   • Continue systemic therapy (e.g., additional cycles of FOLFOXIRI or switch to a regimen incorporating targeted agents based on molecular profile) for further downsizing.  
   • Re‑image after 2–3 cycles and reassess resectability.  
- Post‑operative management:  
   • Pathology review to confirm margin status and presence/absence of viable tumor.  
   • Resume adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., 3–6 months) tailored to final pathology and molecular markers.  
   • Schedule regular surveillance (CEA, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI every 3–6 months for the first 2 years).  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact number, size, and segmental distribution of the original liver metastases.  
- Baseline and post‑treatment liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, ICG clearance, future liver remnant volume).  
- Current status of the primary rectal tumor (clinical T/N stage, whether it has been resected or requires neoadjuvant radiotherapy).  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status).  
- Patient’s performance status and comorbidities influencing surgical risk.  
- Details of the imaging protocol used for the “complete disappearance” (CT slice thickness, contrast phase, use of liver‑specific sequences).  
- Any evidence of extra‑hepatic disease beyond the liver (e.g., lung nodules, peritoneal implants).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bilobar liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, CT shows complete radiological disappearance of all lesions and CEA has normalized. Despite this apparent complete response, the high risk of occult residual microscopic disease at the sites of the initial metastases makes the situation potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but not safely classifiable as disease-free without precise remapping of the original disease.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion-weighted sequences and compare meticulously with baseline imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, even if no lesion is currently visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach targeting the original metastatic locations, not only visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to detect occult residual disease.
• Depending on distribution, a staged approach may be required.

C. If surgical targeting of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and close imaging surveillance.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal strategy.

D. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• If surgery is performed, resume systemic therapy to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial lesions on baseline imaging.
B. Precise localization of the initial metastases relative to vascular structures.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor : circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
E. Patient’s performance status for potential staged hepatectomy.
F. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
- Completeness: Both recommendations encompass the major clinical domains necessary for managing colorectal cancer with liver metastases, including assessment of resectability, preoperative staging, surgical management, systemic therapy, and postoperative management. They both emphasize the importance of detailed imaging and functional assessments before declaring lesions resectable or disease-free.

- Step-by-step concordance: Both recommendations follow the same general steps: assessing resectability after systemic therapy, utilizing advanced imaging techniques to ensure precise location mapping of original lesions, followed by a surgical strategy informed by imaging and potential continuation of systemic therapy if surgery isn't feasible.

- Case-tailoring concordance: Both recommendations take into account case-specific elements, such as molecular profile, lesion-specific surgical considerations, and patient-level factors like performance status and surgical risk.

- Missing data concordance: Both identify similar critical missing data such as detailed imaging for the original metastases, future liver remnant, and performance status. Moreover, both highlight the absence of extrahepatic disease as a critical factor and emphasize the need for precise localization of the initial metastases in relation to vascular structures.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, history of bisegmentectomy IV-V. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VII (3.9 cm). No other lesion at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Late isolated recurrence, anatomically approachable.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
The solitary 3.9 cm metastasis in segment VII is amenable to a parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomy or wedge resection. Prior bisegmentectomy IV‑V has left segments I‑III, VI, VII, VIII; the anticipated future liver remnant will exceed the minimum functional threshold (>30 % in a normal liver, >40 % after prior resection). No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT. KRAS mutation does not affect technical resectability. Therefore the lesion can be removed immediately without prerequisite systemic therapy or additional imaging.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   - Complete liver function panel (bilirubin, INR, albumin), indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin scan to confirm adequate hepatic reserve.  
   - Volumetric CT or MRI to quantify future liver remnant; ensure >40 % of total liver volume.  
   - Baseline CEA and performance‑status assessment (ECOG 0‑1).  
   - Review prior systemic therapy (if any) and assess cumulative oxaliplatin exposure.  

2. Surgical plan (first‑line)  
   - Proceed to curative‑intent liver resection within 4–6 weeks after work‑up.  
   - Preferred approach: laparoscopic or open segmentectomy of segment VII with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion margins and exclude occult disease.  
   - Aim for R0 resection (≥1 cm margin when feasible; ≤5 mm acceptable if anatomy limits).  
   - Employ parenchymal‑sparing techniques (e.g., selective inflow/outflow control, ultrasonic dissection) to preserve maximal liver tissue.  

3. Post‑operative management  
   - Standard enhanced recovery pathway; monitor liver function daily.  
   - Pathology review for margin status, tumor‑grade, and response.  

4. Adjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Initiate adjuvant chemotherapy within 8–12 weeks post‑op, provided recovery is adequate.  
   - Recommended regimen: 6 months of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) – anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective with KRAS mutation.  
   - Consider adding bevacizumab only if high‑risk features (e.g., >3 cm, vascular invasion) and no contraindications.  

5. Surveillance  
   - CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  
   - Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Current liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count).  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume (CT/MRI volumetry).  
- Performance status and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Prior systemic chemotherapy regimens and cumulative doses.  
- Baseline tumor marker (CEA) level.  
- Details of the prior bisegmentectomy (extent of vascular control, any postoperative complications).  

These data are needed to confirm operative safety and to tailor the peri‑operative chemotherapy plan, but the available information already supports an upfront resection.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single metachronous liver metastasis in segment VII (3.9 cm) after a prior bisegmentectomy IV–V, without reported extrahepatic disease. The lesion is located in a posterior segment and appears anatomically accessible while preserving adequate inflow/outflow and functional reserve. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of prior limited hepatectomy, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative vascular and volumetric assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of segment VII.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (current liver) and confirm preservation of portal inflow and hepatic venous outflow.

B. Consider peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the KRAS mutation and recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) may be considered to address potential micrometastatic disease.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.

D. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing)
• Proceed with an ultrasound-guided wedge/segmental resection of segment VII aiming for R0 margins while preserving maximal functional parenchyma.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both approaches.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles if administered.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information

Man, 64 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with four bilobar liver metastases. CEA 900 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. Liver MRI: segment VII lesion invading the IVC over 1 cm.
MDT Discussion: Caval invasion requiring multidisciplinary surgical evaluation.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The patient has four bilobar liver metastases, which can be cleared surgically if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be secured.  
- The segment VII lesion invades the inferior vena cava (IVC) over a length of >1 cm, a situation that typically requires IVC segmental resection and vascular reconstruction, which is technically feasible only after careful multidisciplinary planning.  
- Because the IVC involvement mandates complex vascular surgery and the need to ensure sufficient FLR (potentially after portal vein embolization), a prerequisite systemic therapy to assess tumor biology and possibly downsize the lesions is required before definitive resection.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy: FOLFOXIRI plus anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type status; aim for 2–3 months (4–6 cycles).  
- Re‑stage with contrast‑enhanced MRI/CT and repeat IVC imaging (CT venography or MR venography) after chemotherapy to evaluate response of liver lesions and extent of IVC invasion.  
- If disease remains confined to liver and IVC involvement is still limited to a resectable segment, proceed with multidisciplinary surgical planning:  
   • Perform left hemicolectomy (or oncologic resection of the primary) either synchronously or staged, depending on patient fitness.  
   • Assess FLR; if <30 % of total liver volume, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) of the future liver remnant to induce hypertrophy, waiting 4–6 weeks for adequate growth.  
   • Plan liver resection with en‑bloc segment VII tumor resection and IVC segmental resection; reconstruct IVC using a ring‑reinforced PTFE graft or autologous vein conduit, with intra‑operative heparinisation and postoperative anticoagulation protocol.  
   • Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm negative margins and to guide parenchymal transection; consider Pringle maneuver as needed.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen or continuation of systemic therapy) for at least 3 months, tailored to pathological response and margin status.  
- Enroll patient in a structured surveillance program (CEA, imaging every 3–6 months) for early detection of recurrence.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Current performance status (ECOG/ASA) and cardiopulmonary reserve to tolerate major hepatic‑vascular surgery.  
- Baseline liver function tests and indocyanine green clearance or similar assessment of hepatic functional reserve.  
- Precise volumetric measurement of future liver remnant.  
- Detailed characterization of IVC invasion (circumferential involvement, degree of lumen compromise, proximity to hepatic veins).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., peritoneal, pulmonary metastases).  
- BRAF mutation status and microsatellite instability, which may influence systemic therapy choices.  
- Patient’s preferences regarding aggressive surgical approaches.

• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
